newsitem.title: USA: Annan calls for end to name-calling over U.N..
newsitem.headline: Annan calls for end to name-calling over U.N..

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan called on Friday for an end to name-calling involving the United Nations and promised to submit a package of reforms to next September's session of the General Assembly.

"My report on United Nations reform will be completed by the end of July 1997, at which point I will initiate consultations with member states and submit proposals to the General Assembly at its 52nd session," he said in a speech to the National Press Club.

Reform has been a constant theme of the Ghanaian diplomat's visit to Washington, his first to any capital since taking office on Jan. 1. It has figured prominently at his meetings with U.S. President Bill Clinton, congressmen, senators and other leaders.

Annan's path to election was cleared after the United States vetoed a second term for his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who Washington charged had failed to press reform of the 185-nation organisation with sufficient vigour.

"Today, I ask for partnership. I ask for rededication and reaffirmation of the ideals of the U.N. Charter," Annan said, seeking to open a new chapter in relations between the United Nations and its most powerful founding member.
"Where we have differences, let us address them openly and honestly. But let us at last put an end to the accusations, counter-accusations, and name-calling," he said.

Calling his meetings in Washington "constructive and positive," he said he had assured U.S. leaders of his determination to reform the world body. "Not reform for its own sake, but in order to revitalise the organisation's capacity to serve its members in our changing world."
Borrowing a catch-phrase from Clinton's recent re-election campaign, he added: "We, too, cannot risk falling off the bridge to the 21st century.

"We have already begun our journey across that bridge," he said, reeling off a string of reforms that he said had already been carried out. They included a 25 percent reduction in senior U.N. staff since 1992, capping the two-year U.N. budget at a no-growth figure of $2.6 billion and embarking on more than 400 efficiency projects.

On the issue of U.N. dues, for which the United States is assessed a 25 percent share and even more for peacekeeping, he said the scale was agreed with the rest of the world and was based principally on each nation's share in the world economy.
"If you were a poorer country, the United Nations would ask you for less. But the formula is not sacrosanct."

The United States could negotiate for a lower scale "but it must persuade other member states first," he said, implicitly criticising unilateral moves by Congress to set a lower rate for its contributions.
Washington currently owes the United Nations more than $1 billion in unpaid budget dues and peacekeeping costs.

Without specifically mentioning the U.S. debt, Annan said the crisis facing the United Nations could not be dealt with by "tinkering with the budget or using better cash management techniques. It is rather a political crisis -- a crisis of faith in the organisation."
